title: Six weeks of work, and the experiment came back flat
summary: No significant difference on the primary metric. The team wants to ship anyway. Decide what the result actually supports.

brief.role: You are the PM for the discovery surface of a marketplace app.
brief.company: Harborside, a consumer marketplace for secondhand furniture with 2.1m monthly active users.
brief.context: Six weeks ago the team shipped a new recommendation module on the home screen into a 50/50 A/B test. The primary metric was purchases per visitor. The test has now run for four weeks and the result is flat: +0.4% with a confidence interval spanning -1.1% to +1.9%. The designer and the engineering lead both want to ship it — it looks better, it is faster, and two secondary metrics moved. Your analytics partner says the test 'did not detect an effect'. The head of product asks you what you want to do at Thursday's review.
brief.objective: Make a decision the team can defend afterwards, whichever way it goes.
brief.constraints: Keeping the test running costs nothing directly, but the module is blocking two other home-screen changes that are queued behind it. The analytics partner is available for one more analysis this week.
brief.task: Decide what to do with the module and be explicit about what the data does and does not support.

evidenceCards.title: Experiment results
evidenceCards.content:
Four weeks, 1.04m visitors per arm.

Primary metric — purchases per visitor: +0.4% (95% CI: -1.1% to +1.9%). Not significant.

Secondary metrics:
- Items viewed per session: +6.2% (CI +4.8% to +7.6%). Significant.
- Saves per visitor: +3.1% (CI +1.4% to +4.8%). Significant.
- Home screen load time: -180ms. Significant.
- Sessions per visitor: +0.2% (CI -0.9% to +1.3%). Not significant.
- Seller contact rate: -2.4% (CI -4.0% to -0.8%). Significant, and in the wrong direction.

Analytics partner's note: 'The test was powered to detect a 2% change in purchases per visitor at 80% power. We got 0.4% with a CI that includes 2%, so we can neither claim it works nor rule out an effect we would have cared about. Seven secondary metrics means roughly a one in three chance at least one crosses significance by luck alone; I would not treat any single secondary as a finding on its own.'

evidenceCards.title: What the module changed
evidenceCards.content:
The new module replaces a static 'Recently listed' row with a personalised 'Picked for you' carousel of 12 items, driven by the existing recommendation service. It also loads asynchronously, which is where the 180ms improvement comes from.

One behavioural change the team did not anticipate: the new carousel sits above the 'Message seller' shortcut that previously appeared in the first screenful. On phones under 6 inches the shortcut is now below the fold. The engineering lead thinks this explains the seller contact drop and estimates two days to move it back above the carousel.

The recommendation service itself was not changed. If the module ships, the service becomes load-bearing for the home screen; it currently has no dedicated on-call and a 99.2% availability record over the last quarter.

evidenceCards.title: Segment analysis
evidenceCards.content:
The analytics partner ran an unplanned segment breakdown after the flat result came in.

Purchases per visitor by user tenure:
- New visitors (first session): +4.1% (CI +1.2% to +7.0%)
- Returning, under 3 months: +0.9% (CI -1.8% to +3.6%)
- Returning, over 3 months: -1.6% (CI -3.4% to +0.2%)

Partner's note, verbatim: 'This was not a pre-registered analysis and I ran six segment cuts before showing you this one. Treat it as a hypothesis for a new test, not as a result. The direction is plausible — personalisation should help people with no browsing history least, and these numbers say the opposite, which is worth understanding before anyone builds on it.'

evidenceCards.title: Team and roadmap context
evidenceCards.content:
The two changes queued behind this module are a category navigation redesign (four weeks of work, already built, waiting for a clean home screen to test against) and a seller-side promotion slot (a revenue initiative with a committed number attached to it this quarter).

The designer's position: 'The old row was static and ugly. Even flat, the new one is better and it is faster.'
The engineering lead's position: 'We built it, it works, holding it in a flag has a cost. Ship it.'
The head of product has not stated a position and has previously said she values 'decisions we can defend six months later'.

No commitment has been made externally about this module. It is not on any roadmap shown to customers.

decisionPrompt: What do you do with the recommendation module?

decisionOptions.label: Fix the seller shortcut, ship, and register the new-visitor question as its own test
decisionOptions.description: Spend two days moving the 'Message seller' shortcut back above the fold, ship the module on the strength of engagement and speed rather than purchases, and pre-register a test of the new-visitor effect.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The shortcut fix ships with the module. Seller contact rate returns to baseline within a week; items viewed and saves hold their gains; purchases per visitor stays flat, as expected.
The home screen is unblocked and the category navigation test starts two weeks later. The pre-registered new-visitor test runs the following month and comes back at +2.2% for first-session visitors, significant — a real finding the team can build on.
At the six-month review the decision reads well: shipped for stated reasons, fixed a known regression, and turned an exploratory cut into a proper result.
Trade-off: you shipped something that did not move the metric you set out to move, and you were explicit about that rather than reframing the goal.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Strongest when the rationale separates 'no detected effect' from 'no effect', refuses to treat the segment cut as a result, addresses the seller-contact regression, and is honest that shipping is justified by speed and engagement, not by the primary metric.

decisionOptions.label: Ship it and report the secondary metrics as the win
decisionOptions.description: Items viewed is up 6.2% and saves are up 3.1%, both significant. Ship and present those as the result.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The module ships and the review goes smoothly. Two months later, in a quarterly business review, someone asks why engagement is up and purchases are not, and the honest answer surfaces along with the seller contact regression, which nobody fixed and which has quietly cost an estimated 1.5% of transactions.
The analytics partner is asked whether the secondary metrics were pre-registered. They were not the primary. The head of product's confidence in the team's experiment reporting drops noticeably, and the next two experiments get extra scrutiny.
Trade-off: you got the outcome you wanted this week and spent credibility and a real metric to do it.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Weak. Promoting secondary metrics to the headline after a flat primary is the specific failure mode here, and it ignores the significant regression in seller contact.

decisionOptions.label: Kill the module
decisionOptions.description: The primary metric did not move and a secondary metric regressed. Roll back and unblock the queue.
decisionOptions.consequence:
The module is removed. The home screen returns to the static row, 180ms slower, and the two queued initiatives start immediately.
Six weeks of work is discarded, including a faster home screen and a real engagement gain. The designer takes it badly. In the retro the team notes that no one asked whether the seller shortcut regression was fixable — it was, in two days.
The new-visitor signal is never followed up, because the module it depended on no longer exists.
Trade-off: you applied the primary metric strictly and threw away improvements the test did measure, along with a promising lead.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Defensible discipline, but the evidence contains a two-day fix for the regression and significant gains elsewhere. Credit when the rationale engages with those and rejects them for a stated reason.

decisionOptions.label: Run the test longer to reach significance
decisionOptions.description: The confidence interval still includes a 2% effect. Keep the test running for another four weeks to narrow it.
decisionOptions.consequence:
Four more weeks doubles the sample. The primary metric lands at +0.6% with a CI of -0.4% to +1.6% — still not significant, and now confidently excluding the 2% effect the team hoped for.
The answer is genuinely clearer. It also cost four weeks of the category navigation test and delayed the seller promotion slot, which misses its quarterly number by two weeks of runway.
The seller contact regression ran for four extra weeks on 50% of traffic.
Trade-off: you bought a sharper answer to a question whose two possible answers pointed to the same action.
decisionOptions.rubricNote: Statistically reasonable and worth partial credit for wanting to narrow the interval. Mark down when the rationale does not ask whether a sharper estimate would change the decision, and when it leaves the regression running.

rubric.referenceReasoning: A flat result is not a null result — the interval spans -1.1% to +1.9%, so an effect the team would have cared about has not been excluded, and neither has no effect. That means the primary metric cannot justify shipping and cannot justify killing. What the test did measure well: a 180ms speed improvement, a significant engagement gain, and a significant regression in seller contact that the engineering note explains and offers a two-day fix for. Those are real, and they are a legitimate basis for a decision as long as they are described as what they are rather than promoted into the headline the primary metric failed to deliver. The segment cut is the trap: it was unplanned, one of six, and the partner explicitly says it is a hypothesis. A strong answer ships or kills on the honestly-stated grounds, fixes the regression first, and converts the segment finding into a pre-registered test rather than a claim.
evidenceSignals: Distinguishes 'no detected effect' from 'no effect' using the confidence interval
Notes the test was powered for 2% and the interval still includes 2%
Treats the seller contact regression as a real, significant, and fixable finding
Recognises the segment analysis was unplanned and one of six cuts
Accounts for multiple-comparison risk across seven secondary metrics
Notices the module makes the recommendation service load-bearing without on-call coverage

product_sense: Judges the module on the value it demonstrably delivers rather than the value it was hoped to deliver
Notices that above-the-fold real estate was reallocated and that this had a cost
analytics: Reads the confidence interval rather than only the point estimate or the p-value
Refuses to promote secondary metrics to a headline after a flat primary
Treats an exploratory segment cut as a hypothesis and proposes pre-registering it
Asks whether a narrower interval would actually change the decision
user_research: Uses the mechanism explanation for the seller-contact drop rather than treating it as noise
prioritization: Weighs the cost of holding the queue against the value of a sharper estimate
execution: Fixes the known regression before or alongside shipping
Notes the operational dependency the module creates on the recommendation service
communication: States plainly what the experiment did and did not show
Gives a recommendation that will still read well in six months

product_sense: Ships because the team built it and it looks better, with no stated basis
analytics: Treats a flat result as proof of no effect
Reports a significant secondary as the experiment's result
Treats the unplanned segment cut as a finding rather than a hypothesis
Ignores the multiple-comparison caveat the partner gave explicitly
execution: Ships without addressing the significant seller-contact regression
Extends the test while a known regression continues on half of traffic
communication: Frames the outcome to match what the team wanted rather than what was measured

learnTakeaway.title: Read the interval, not the verdict
learnTakeaway.body: 'Not significant' answers a narrower question than most teams think: it says the data did not rule out zero. The confidence interval says what the data did rule out. When the interval still contains the effect size you designed the test for, you have learned less than the flat headline suggests — and the honest options are to power up, or to decide on other grounds and say so. The one move to avoid is promoting a secondary metric into the headline slot, because it converts an inconclusive test into a claim you cannot defend later.

qaSubmissions.label: strong
qaSubmissions.rationale: Flat isn't null. We powered for 2%, got +0.4%, and the interval runs to +1.9% — so we haven't detected an effect and haven't excluded one we'd care about. The primary metric can't carry either decision, and I'd say that rather than reach for a secondary. What we did measure: 180ms faster, +6.2% items viewed, and a real -2.4% seller contact regression the carousel explains. Two days to move the shortcut back, then ship — on speed and engagement, explicitly not on purchases. The tenure cut was one of six unplanned analyses; I'd pre-register a new-visitor test rather than quote it in the review.

qaSubmissions.label: defensible_alternative
qaSubmissions.rationale: Roll it back — a judgement call, not something the data forces. We set purchases per visitor as the primary metric precisely so we wouldn't argue afterwards, and it didn't move. Items viewed and saves are engagement, and on a marketplace where people browse a lot and buy rarely, more browsing isn't self-evidently good. Meanwhile seller contact is down 2.4% significantly. The shortcut fix is two days, but then we're shipping a module whose only demonstrated benefit is 180ms we could get from the async load alone. I'd keep the new-visitor question as a pre-registered test.

qaSubmissions.label: weak
qaSubmissions.rationale: Items viewed is up 6.2% and saves are up 3.1%, both statistically significant, and the page is 180ms faster. Purchases were up 0.4% too, just not significant, so the direction is positive across the board. We should ship it and report the engagement wins.
